title: Tricky Endgame: Keep the Pawn on h6
summary: Choose a one-square pawn move so the king can support a knight sacrifice and stop the opponent’s promotion.

nodes.question: Which pawn move preserves Black’s win?
nodes.explanation: Black has Kc5/Ne8/h7 against White Ke5/g6. Black is to move. Keeping the extra knight is less important than stopping White’s advanced pawn.

branches.title: Advance one square, then offer the knight
commentary: Black has Kc5/Ne8/h7 against White Ke5/g6. Black is to move. Keeping the extra knight is less important than stopping White’s advanced pawn.
h6 is the only winning move in this exact diagram. It preserves the king-and-knight coordination that the immediate h5 advance loses.
Ke6 ignores the h-pawn and approaches Ne8. This is the source’s critical alternative.
Kd4 centralizes the king before the knight is attacked.
Kf7 attacks Ne8 and supports the g-pawn’s promotion square.
Ke5 offers the knight: Black is preparing to reach f6 rather than spending a tempo saving the piece.
Kxe8 takes the knight, but White’s king has been drawn away from g6.
Kf6 stops the g-pawn’s effective promotion route. The exact king-and-pawn ending is winning for Black despite the lost knight; later pawn conversion remains outside this branch.

branches.title: Independent legal continuation of the king chase
commentary: Black has Kc5/Ne8/h7 against White Ke5/g6. Black is to move. Keeping the extra knight is less important than stopping White’s advanced pawn.
h6 preserves the win while controlling g5.
Kf5 approaches the h-pawn.
Kd4 brings Black’s king closer to the action.
Kg4 continues toward the pawn.
Ng7 controls f5 and h5; together with h6’s control of g5 it blocks the approach. This move is not check in this diagram.
Kh4 stays near the pawn. From this point the king route is an independently selected representative continuation.
Ke5 improves Black’s king while the knight and pawn hold the barrier.
Kg4 waits near the kingside without gaining access to h6.
Kf6 approaches White’s g6 pawn.
Kh4 maintains the same waiting route.
Kxg6 removes White’s last pawn. Black retains an exact win with king, knight and h-pawn; the full conversion is not assumed from material alone.

branches.title: Capturing the pawn gives away the win
commentary: Black has Kc5/Ne8/h7 against White Ke5/g6. Black is to move. Keeping the extra knight is less important than stopping White’s advanced pawn.
hxg6 removes White’s pawn but gives up the forced win. Black’s surviving g-pawn can be caught.
Kf4 approaches the pawn’s stopping squares. The captions say Kf5, but that square is attacked by the black pawn on g6 and is illegal here.
g5+ is an independently selected representative pawn push, giving check to the king on f4.
Kxg5 removes the last pawn. King and knight cannot force mate against the lone king; this exact position is drawn.

branches.title: The fast h-pawn lets both sides promote
commentary: Black has Kc5/Ne8/h7 against White Ke5/g6. Black is to move. Keeping the extra knight is less important than stopping White’s advanced pawn.
h5 advances too far and gives up the exact win.
Kf5 heads toward the advanced pawn.
Ng7+ defends h5 and checks the king on f5.
Kg5 approaches the pawn again.
Kd4 brings the king closer, but the knight and pawn can no longer form the h6 barrier.
Kh6 attacks the knight on g7.
h4 runs the pawn and abandons the knight.
Kxg7 captures the knight, freeing White’s own promotion race.
h3 continues toward h1.
Kf7 supports the g-pawn’s promotion route.
h2 is one step from promotion.
g7 starts White’s final push.
h1=Q promotes first, but the queen gives no immediate check.
g8=Q gives White a queen too. The exact queen ending is drawn with best play; racing first did not preserve Black’s win.

exercises.prompt: Why is h6 stronger than h5?
exercises.answer: The pawn on h6 controls g5 while Ng7 controls f5/h5, keeping the defending king away. If White instead attacks the knight, Black has time to centralize and stop g6.

exercises.prompt: Why can Black give up Ne8?
exercises.answer: Kxe8 pulls White’s king away. Black reaches f6 and blocks the advanced g-pawn, leaving a winning pawn ending.

startContext: The complete five-piece position is reconstructed from the saved physical-board diagrams: Black Kc5/Ne8/h7 and White Ke5/g6, Black to move. The h6/Ke6 knight-sacrifice line and h5 promotion race are illustrated. The longer king-waiting route and the g-pawn capture replies are independently selected legal representatives. Every encoded position is checked; only h6 preserves the exact win at the root.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.

sourceCorrections.correction: The physical board shows the legal Kf4. Kf5 would move into the g6 pawn’s attack, so the encoded comparison uses Kf4.
